drills.q: Design a structure supporting point update and range sum query in O(log n) each, with minimal memory overhead.
drills.a: Fenwick tree (BIT): O(n) space, O(log n) update and prefix-sum query using i & -i to walk ancestor/descendant chains.

drills.q: Why does the Fenwick tree trick fail for range-minimum queries even though the update/query loop structure looks identical?
drills.a: The O(log n) range-query trick relies on being able to subtract one prefix result from another (prefix(r) - prefix(l-1)); min has no inverse operation, so this decomposition is meaningless for min/max.

drills.q: Implement range-add, range-sum query support. What technique do you need beyond a basic segment tree, and why?
drills.a: Lazy propagation -- store a pending delta at the highest fully-covered node instead of pushing it to every leaf immediately; push down only when a future operation must descend past that node. Without it, range updates cost O(n) each.

drills.q: Given a static array and 10 million range-min queries with zero updates, what structure is asymptotically optimal and why not a segment tree?
drills.a: A sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) per query by precomputing min over every power-of-two window and combining two overlapping windows (min is idempotent so overlap is safe). A segment tree would cost O(log n) per query -- strictly worse when there are no updates to justify its flexibility.

drills.q: Derive why the Fenwick tree update and query loops are each bounded by O(log n) steps.
drills.a: Update: i += i & -i strictly increases the trailing-zero-bit count of i each step, bounded by the bit-width of n. Query: i -= i & -i strictly clears the lowest set bit each step, also bounded by bit-width. Both are O(log n).

drills.q: You need k-th smallest element in an arbitrary range [l,r] of a static array, with far more queries than n. What structure, and what's its space complexity?
drills.a: A persistent segment tree (merge sort tree): build a versioned root after inserting each element, and answer k-th-smallest-in-range as a difference between two versions' trees. Each update only touches O(log n) new nodes, so n versions cost O(n log n) total space, not O(n) per version.
